extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, theology, and canonical law; readers of Hobbes' Leviathan
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Hobbes's criteria and arguments concerning the relationship of civil sovereignty and ecclesiastical authority (power to baptize, consecrate, ordain, and limits of papal jurisdiction). Useful for textual analysis, comparative political-theological study, or doctrinal critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian Kings' power to baptize and consecrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Kings have power to Baptize, and to Consecrate both Temples, and Pastors to Gods service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues this follows from the Right of their Office: a sovereign's authority to teach and govern confers the power to perform ecclesiastical acts. He supports with examples (Christ could baptize but deputed the apostles; Paul baptized few because his principal charge was preaching; Solomon consecrated the Temple) to show office-based authorization and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of ministerial acts is compatible with sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the care of the summe of the businesse of the Common-wealth taketh up his whole time, it were not convenient for him to apply himself in Person to that particular ... A King may also if he please, sit in Judgment, to hear and determine all manner of Causes, as well as give others authority to doe it in his name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats delegation as a natural consequence of sovereign duties: a sovereign may delegate baptism, ordination, and judgment without losing the underlying right. He uses the example of Christ and apostles and Paul to illustrate that greater charge excuses direct performance of lesser ministerial acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands is a public designation ceremony, not a metaphysical necessary for authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands ... was a most ancient publique ceremony amongst the Jews, by which was designed, and made certain, the person ... intended in a mans prayer, blessing, sacrifice, consecration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes surveys biblical examples of laying on of hands (Jacob, Aaron, Moses ordaining Joshua, ordination of Levites) to show its function is public designation to assure the eyes. But because sovereigns are already publicly instituted and designated by office (or by baptism), the ceremony is unnecessary to authorize them; imposition is a sign of designation, not the source of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordination/laying on of hands distinguishes designation from conferral of gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: The use then of this ceremony considered in the Ordination of Pastors, was to design the Person to whom they gave such Power ... the Imposition of Hands had been unnecessary; Baptisme it selfe had been sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes the purpose of imposition: to designate persons to office and sometimes to pray for gifts. If a person already possessed authority or had been baptized into office, imposition adds no new power. He cites Acts (Apostles, presbytery laying hands) and Paul's cautions (1 Tim. 5.22) as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign (if Christian) is head of the church in his own dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: From this consolidation of the Right Politique, and Ecclesiastique in Christian Soveraigns, it is evident, they have all manner of Power over their Subjects ... and may make such Laws, as themselves shall judge fittest, for the government of their own Subjects, both as they are the Common-wealth, and as they are the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes claims that State and Church coincide in a Christian commonwealth: the civil sovereign may legislate in matters of religion (externals), appoint church officers, determine maintenance (tithes), and define who are judges/interpreters of canon within his realm. The sovereign's authority is supreme in external actions and words of subjects; matters of conscience (the heart) are for God alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal authority within a sovereign's realm is by civil right (Jure Civili) when delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: If they please therefore, they may (as many Christian Kings now doe) commit the government of their Subjects in matters of Religion to the Pope; but then the Pope is in that point Subordinate to them, and exerciseth that Charge in anothers Dominion Jure Civili, in the Right of the Civill Soveraign; not Jure Divino, in Gods Right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes allows sovereigns to delegate ecclesiastical administration to the Pope or to assemblies of pastors, but emphasizes such delegation makes ecclesiastical authorities subordinate agents of the civil sovereign; their powers derive from the sovereign's civil grant, not from a universal divine grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign appoints interpreters and judges of canonical scripture within his realm
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the Civill Soveraign, that is to appoint Judges, and Interpreters of the Canonicall Scriptures; for it is he that maketh them Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the sovereign makes laws for his subjects, he also establishes who interprets religious law and scripture insofar as those interpretations function as law or guide public practice. This is a claim about institutional competence rather than metaphysical superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's jurisdiction limited to external acts and words; conscience remains God's domain
rubrics_metrics.description: he hath the Supreme Power in all causes, as well Ecclesiasticall, as Civill, as far as concerneth actions, and words, for these onely are known, and may be accused; and of that which cannot be accused, there is no Judg at all, but God, that knoweth the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes draws a boundary: civil authority governs observable behavior and speech; God alone judges internal faith and the heart. This limits what laws sovereigns reasonably may make and enforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying Antichrist (scriptural markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antichrist in the proper signification hath two essentiall marks; One, that he denyeth Jesus to be Christ; and another that he professeth himselfe to bee Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses these marks to argue the Pope is not Antichrist, since the Pope neither denies Jesus nor professes himself to be Christ. This constitutes a doctrinal criterion for classifying false Christs vs political/religious usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texts used to claim papal infallibility must be read in historical/contextual sense
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Infallibility of his Judgments, he alledgeth the Scriptures ... This, according to Bellarmines exposition, is, that Christ gave here to Simon Peter two priviledges ... But he that with attention readeth that chapter, shall find there is no place in the whole Scripture, that maketh more against the Popes Authority, than this very place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes critiques Bellarmine's exegesis (Luke 22, Matth.16, John 21, Exod.28, etc.) arguing that the cited passages more plausibly support limitation to teaching/confession or apply only within particular historical contexts. He endorses close contextual/literal reading: e.g., Matthew 16 refers to the confession (foundation of faith) not a grant of temporal jurisdiction; Luke 22 concerns strengthening brethren after conversion, not perpetual worldly authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between making laws and giving counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Law, is distinguished from Counsell, in this, that the reason of a Law, is taken from the designe, and benefit of him that prescribeth it; but the reason of a Counsell, from the designe, and benefit of him, to whom the Counsell is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses Acts 15 as an example (apostolic 'laying on of burdens' were counsel to aid salvation of converts) to argue that many ecclesiastical pronouncements are advisory for the benefit of recipients, not legislative decrees binding sovereigns or entire commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication without civil sanctions is social denunciation, not civil punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunicate, which (without the Civill Power) is no more but a leaving of their company, and having no more to doe with them, than with a Heathen man, or a Publican; which in many occasions might be a greater pain to the Excommunicant, than to the Excommunicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes that ecclesiastical sanctions (excommunication) have force only insofar as civil power backs them; absent civil enforcement they amount to social or religious exclusion and not to corporeal punishments. Therefore ecclesiastical judges need civil power to make punishments effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural commissions to 'teach' do not equal legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: John 21. ver. 16,17. 'Feed my sheep;' which contains no more but a Commission of Teaching ... Making Laws belongs to the Lord of the Family;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes teaching commissions from law-making authority: biblical injunctions to 'feed' or 'teach' sheep authorize pastoral instruction, but do not confer the power to legislate for temporal societies — that belongs to the civil 'lord of the family' (sovereign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal claim to make laws and punish on earth is incompatible with civil sovereignty of princes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Pope challengeth Supremacy in controversies of Manners, hee teacheth men to disobey the Civill Soveraign; which is an erroneous Doctrine, contrary to the many precepts of our Saviour and his Apostles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that if the Pope claims legislative jurisdiction (making laws and punishments) over subjects of other sovereigns, this conflicts with the scriptural and political obligation to obey temporal sovereigns (Rom.13 etc.). Thus claims of universal papal legislative power are politically and theologically problematic.
